The reference's 326pt frame (:65) is NOT the destination's width: see the Karabiner-Elements entries for why, and record that this file's number was measured against a different window. The group names, the group order and the pages under each group are the daemon's (Host.Group / Host.Order), not the reference's menu sections.
Reason for modification: CrossOS navigates discovered UIContributions rather than an extension list, and its rail is rendered from a webview, so SwiftUI's material, its SF Symbols and its continuous-corner geometry do not transfer. THE SEARCH FIELD AT :102-114 IS DELIBERATELY NOT PORTED and the omission is a decision, not an oversight: the reference's field filters three populations that cannot be enumerated ahead of time — menu actions, the discovered system services and every registered plug-in extension (:499-518) — whereas this rail lists the fifteen settings pages the daemon declares in app/backend, which a person reads in one glance. The closer reference (a macOS settings rail over seventeen items) likewise has no search in it; see the Karabiner-Elements entry. The reference's All/ThisApp/Other segmented filter (:115) is not ported for the same reason: it partitions by SOURCE, a distinction the daemon's page list does not carry. Modification: structural port, no code copied. What transfers is the INTERACTION MODEL and the state machine: a card that is collapsed until asked, whose expansion is owned above it rather than hidden inside the row; a header whose trailing edge carries how many of the members are on (packs.enabledCount, whose English value is "%lld/%lld enabled") so a reader can see how much of the thing is on without opening it; and one switch per member living inside the expanded body rather than on a separate settings page. The reference is SwiftUI on macOS and the destination is React over a declared schema, so the drawing, the icons, the AppIcon and the MMSwitch component do not transfer and none were copied. CrossOS's own vocabulary travels in its place: the members are the profile layer's capabilities (core/pkg/profiles) and the counts come from the daemon's plan arithmetic. Of those counts, the per-capability INPUTS (will_enable, will_enable_plugin, enabled, total) are served by the daemon and the rollups are summed in the control — both the header's "n of m" and the preview sentence — because the selection is a client-side filter over the bundle and the daemon cannot narrow its own answer to a subset it was not told about until the apply. The script executor is NOT copied (§9.11 PARTIAL: menumate is concepts-and-schema-shapes only).
Reason for modification: the reference lists installed third-party extension packs with their contributed menu actions, each of which the user can enable independently and which the import path treats as a bulk write. CrossOS lists its own profile bundles — data declared in-repo, not installed code — and the settings nav has no per-pack settings page to put a duplicate of each member's editor on, so the members' individual verdicts stay on the pages that own them (Keyboard, Windows, Explorer) while the profile's own capabilities get switches here. The boundary is stated once in app/backend/profilespage.go and cited by this destination, because the previous version of this control stated the opposite.

Modification: structural port, no code copied. What transfers is the GATE and its state machine, which is the idea rather than the code: a bulk write that will change several things at once should not be one click away from a list nobody looked at, a row is marked by being looked at rather than by a separate confirmation, and the progress is stated as words under the list so a blocked button is never blocked silently. The reference's own safety target is a script import, and a script is executable code arriving from elsewhere; CrossOS's is a bundle of rules the daemon already has, which is why the gate here is a few lines of state and the reference's is a review screen with a detail pane. The reviewDetail pane, the matchSummary badge, the clone step and the script viewer are NOT ported. The gate is over every available capability rather than over the selection, which the reference's list is by construction — a review set that shrank as rows were deselected would be circular, and that was this control's first implementation. ONE BEHAVIOUR IS A CROSSOS ADDITION and is not a port: the control clears the review set when a card COLLAPSES, where the reference keeps `viewed` for the whole session and assigns a fresh set only on entering the review sheet (:434, a different screen rather than a collapse). The destination is a card on a settings page that can be folded away with its selection still applied in the daemon, so an armed Apply over rows the reader can no longer see is a review of something other than what will be written; the reference has no equivalent hazard because its list cannot be hidden without leaving the sheet. The other defensible rule — that having seen a row is a session-long fact — is the one the reference chose.
Reason for modification: the reference's gate protects against running code the user has not read. The CrossOS equivalent risk is a bulk settings write the user has not seen, so the same viewed-set state machine gates the Apply; the difference in stakes is why no detail pane came with it, and why a disabled Apply always carries its sentence on the page rather than only in a title attribute. The two failure modes the port inherits from the reference are kept deliberately — a stuck gate that cannot be cleared, and a row that never marks — because the reference resolves both by making the review gesture and the mark the same click.

What makes the reference the right source is that it is the only surface in that repository answering the question this page answers — how much of a list of things a person must get through is left, shown rather than counted — and it answers it with a mark per row, one card, and one number under the card. The mark's SOURCE is the difference that matters: there the tick is an acknowledgement the reader gives, here it is a verdict the daemon asserts, and a wizard that showed its own ticks would be claiming a machine is set up when the daemon has not said so.

Original license: MIT
Original copyright: Copyright (c) 2026 Hibrielle
CrossOS destination: app/frontend/public/style.css (--hairline and --done in :root, the dark-mode --done step, the .ctl-list and .ctl-steps card backgrounds, and the .ctl-step-mark ring and fill)
Modification: structural port, and the constants are COPIED where the reference states them: the 0.7 opacity of --hairline and the 0.5 hairline width are the reference's own numbers and are taken as such. The COLOURS are not copied because the reference stores none: MMColor.card, separator and green are all AppKit/SwiftUI SEMANTIC colours resolved against the user's settings, and this stylesheet's existing answer to that is the same one it documents at length above (:55-104) — hand the resolution back to the OS, --bg-sunken is already ButtonFace which is controlBackgroundColor, --line is already the border keyword, and --hairline is the reference's 0.7 applied to whichever of those the theme resolved. --done is the one token here with a literal in the destination and NO literal in the reference: MMColor.green is Color.green, so the value written is macOS's own system green rather than anything from that repository, and it is the mark beside a done step, which is decoration next to the "Done" chip and so is not held to the 4.5:1 rule the file records for --live. --done is deliberately NOT --live: --live means the machine is recording you now (documented at the top of :root) and reusing it for a completed setup step would make a green mark mean two things on one screen.
Reason for modification: SwiftUI semantic colours have no single hex to copy, and this shell is not entitled to invent one when the OS will resolve the same name — so the tokens are either bridged or, where no CSS system colour exists, recorded as a literal with the reason stated in the stylesheet.
CrossOS license: MIT

CrossOS destination: app/frontend/src/controls/ChecklistControl.tsx (ReadinessLine — the two-line row, the chip as the only tone carrier, and the daemon's raw `detail` kept on the row in `title` and drawn in the dimmer voice underneath), app/frontend/src/controls/WizardControl.tsx (StepReason, the same two lines for a first-run step's own reason)
Modification: structural port, no code copied. What transfers is the SHAPE of a stated state: a mark that is never in the words, a description on its own line under the title, a refusal in a different voice from a not-yet, and a state with no door named as having no door. NO constant, string or formula was taken: the destination's line heights, spacing, colours and corner radii are its own existing stylesheet, the vocabulary is the destination's own (ctl-item + is-block for the stacking, ctl-chip for the mark, ctl-value for the state, ctl-empty for the sub-line), and every shipped sentence in readinessReasons.ts was WRITTEN for CrossOS rather than translated — the reference's English strings are quoted in that file's header comment as the model for the voice and are not the copy. One reference string IS quoted verbatim, in a test name and the comment above it: "Extension not registered (run the main app once first)", from App/Localizable.xcstrings (see the block below). The page names the sentences point at (Safety, Extensions, Profiles, Shortcuts, Activity) are the DAEMON's own titles, read from app/backend/pages.go's contrib() calls and app/backend/profilespage.go:38, not the reference's, and the two System Settings grants the permission sentence names are the daemon's own strings (core/internal/adapter/tap_cgo.go:43 names Input Monitoring; core/cmd/crossos/main.go:469's accessibilityPane and its :468-470 comment say Accessibility) — the destination names both because the daemon disagrees with itself, and neither word came from this repository.
Reason for modification: the reference is a SwiftUI onboarding flow with three fixed steps and a set of known permissions; the destination renders a declared schema over a daemon whose readiness reasons are Go error values, and a missing renderer is a defect somebody has to find rather than a flow step. The reference supplies the treatment of a state; the sentences themselves are the destination's, and a shell that translated them would be shipping another app's copy over somebody's own machine.
